title: Numerical Solution of Equations Module 1 Lesson 1: Graphical Existence and Uniqueness custom practice

evidence_basis.originality_note: All prompts, values and combinations are original; mapped Cambridge evidence informs scope and assessment structure only.

parts.prompt: On a single diagram, sketch the graphs of $y = \ln x$ and $y = 3 - x$. Hence state the number of real roots of the equation $\ln x = 3 - x$.

figure.purpose: Show the intersection of the natural logarithm curve and downward sloping linear graph.
figure.alt_text: Graph showing y = ln x and y = 3 - x intersecting at one point.
figure.brief: Draw Cartesian axes with x > 0. Sketch y = ln x passing through (1,0) with vertical asymptote x = 0. Sketch straight line y = 3 - x with intercepts (0,3) and (3,0). Mark single intersection point clearly.

parts.prompt: By sketching the curves $y = \mathrm{e}^x$ and $y = \dfrac{2}{x}$ for $x > 0$, explain why the equation $x\mathrm{e}^x = 2$ has exactly one positive real root.

figure.purpose: Show the intersection of exponential growth and reciprocal curve in the first quadrant.
figure.alt_text: Graph showing y = e^x and y = 2/x in first quadrant with one intersection.
figure.brief: Draw first quadrant axes. Sketch increasing exponential curve y = e^x starting at (0,1). Sketch decreasing hyperbola y = 2/x approaching axes as asymptotes. Show single point of intersection.

parts.prompt: Sketch the graphs of $y = x^2$ and $y = \dfrac{4}{x}$ for all real $x \neq 0$. Deduce the number of real roots of $x^3 = 4$.

figure.purpose: Show parabola y = x^2 and hyperbola y = 4/x intersecting only in the first quadrant.
figure.alt_text: Graph showing y = x^2 and y = 4/x across both positive and negative x.
figure.brief: Draw full Cartesian plane. Sketch parabola y = x^2 vertex at origin. Sketch hyperbola y = 4/x in quadrants 1 and 3. Show one intersection in quadrant 1 and none in quadrant 3.

parts.prompt: On a single sketch for $0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi$, draw $y = \cos x$ and $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x$. State the number of real roots of $\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}x$ in this interval.

figure.purpose: Show cosine curve and straight line intersecting in [0, pi].
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = cos x and y = 0.5x from x = 0 to pi.
figure.brief: Draw axes for x in [0, pi]. Sketch y = cos x from (0,1) through (pi/2, 0) to (pi, -1). Sketch line y = 0.5x through (0,0) and (pi, pi/2). Indicate single intersection point before pi/2.

parts.prompt: Sketch $y = \tan x$ and $y = 2 - x$ for $0 \leqslant x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Explain why the equation $\tan x + x = 2$ has a unique root in the interval $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

figure.purpose: Show tangent curve and decreasing line intersecting once in [0, pi/2).
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = tan x and y = 2 - x for 0 <= x < pi/2.
figure.brief: Draw axes for 0 <= x < pi/2 with dashed vertical asymptote at x = pi/2. Sketch y = tan x increasing from (0,0). Sketch y = 2 - x decreasing from (0,2) to (pi/2, 2 - pi/2). Indicate single intersection.

parts.prompt: By sketching $y = \mathrm{e}^{-x}$ and $y = x^3$ for $x > 0$, show graphically that the equation $x^3\mathrm{e}^x = 1$ has exactly one positive real root.

figure.purpose: Show decaying exponential and cubic curve intersecting at exactly one point.
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = e^(-x) and y = x^3 for x > 0.
figure.brief: Draw first quadrant axes. Sketch decaying exponential y = e^(-x) from (0,1) towards x-axis. Sketch cubic y = x^3 from (0,0) steeply increasing. Show single intersection point.

questions.prompt: The equation $2\ln(x + 1) = 5 - x$ is to be solved.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: On a single diagram, sketch the graphs of $y = 2\ln(x + 1)$ and $y = 5 - x$, showing the coordinates of the points where each graph crosses the axes and any asymptotes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce that the equation $2\ln(x + 1) = 5 - x$ has a unique positive root $\alpha$, and state an integer $n$ such that $n < \alpha < n + 1$.

figure.purpose: Show the shifted natural logarithm curve and downward sloping straight line.
figure.alt_text: Graph showing y = 2ln(x+1) and y = 5-x intersecting in the first quadrant.
figure.brief: Axes from x = -1.5 to 6. Vertical asymptote x = -1. Curve y = 2ln(x+1) passing through origin (0,0) and increasing. Line y = 5-x passing through (0,5) and (5,0). Show intersection point between x = 2 and x = 3.

questions.prompt: Consider the equation $\sec x = 3 - x$ in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Sketch the graphs of $y = \sec x$ and $y = 3 - x$ on the same axes for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the equation $\sec x = 3 - x$ has exactly two real roots in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, one positive and one negative.

figure.purpose: Show secant curve and straight line with two intersection points in (-pi/2, pi/2).
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = sec x and y = 3 - x for -pi/2 < x < pi/2.
figure.brief: Axes with -pi/2 < x < pi/2 and vertical asymptotes x = -pi/2 and x = pi/2. Curve y = sec x symmetrical about y-axis with minimum at (0,1). Line y = 3 - x passing through (0,3). Intersections at x < 0 and x > 0.

questions.prompt: The equation $x\mathrm{e}^{2x} = 5$ is to be analyzed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Show that for $x > 0$, the equation $x\mathrm{e}^{2x} = 5$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{e}^{2x} = \dfrac{5}{x}$. Sketch the curves $y = \mathrm{e}^{2x}$ and $y = \dfrac{5}{x}$ on the same diagram for $x > 0$, and state the number of positive roots.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: By considering the sign of $x\mathrm{e}^{2x}$ for $x < 0$, explain why $x\mathrm{e}^{2x} = 5$ has no negative real roots.

figure.purpose: Show exponential curve y = e^(2x) and hyperbola y = 5/x in quadrant 1.
figure.alt_text: Graph showing y = e^(2x) and y = 5/x for x > 0.
figure.brief: First quadrant axes. Sketch y = e^(2x) increasing from (0,1). Sketch y = 5/x decreasing towards x-axis. Single intersection point in quadrant 1.

questions.prompt: The equation $x^2\ln x = 2$ has a root $\alpha$ for $x > 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: By sketching the curves $y = \ln x$ and $y = \dfrac{2}{x^2}$ for $x > 0$, prove that the equation $x^2\ln x = 2$ has exactly one real root $\alpha$, and show that $\alpha > 1$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: By evaluating the values of $\ln x$ and $\dfrac{2}{x^2}$ at $x = \mathrm{e}$, determine whether $\alpha < \mathrm{e}$ or $\alpha > \mathrm{e}$.

figure.purpose: Show y = ln x and y = 2/x^2 intersecting once at x in (1, e).
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = ln x and y = 2/x^2 showing intersection alpha between 1 and e.
figure.brief: Axes for x > 0. Sketch y = ln x crossing x-axis at (1,0) and passing through (e,1). Sketch y = 2/x^2 passing through (1,2) and (e, 2/e^2). Intersection clearly in (1, e).

questions.prompt: Consider the equation $2\cot x = x^2 - 1$ in the interval $0 < x < \pi$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Sketch the graphs of $y = 2\cot x$ and $y = x^2 - 1$ on the same diagram for $0 < x < \pi$, showing all vertical asymptotes and axis intercepts.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the equation $2\cot x = x^2 - 1$ has a unique root $\alpha$ in $0 < x < \pi$, and determine which of the three intervals $(0, 1)$, $\left(1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, or $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$ contains $\alpha$.

figure.purpose: Show cotangent curve and parabola on (0, pi) with intersection in (1, pi/2).
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = 2cot x and y = x^2 - 1 for 0 < x < pi.
figure.brief: Axes for 0 < x < pi with vertical asymptotes x = 0 and x = pi. Sketch cotangent curve crossing x-axis at (pi/2, 0). Sketch parabola y = x^2 - 1 vertex (0,-1) crossing x-axis at (1,0). Intersection clearly marked in (1, pi/2).

questions.prompt: The curve $C$ has equation $y = x\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ for all real $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $C$. Hence sketch the curve $y = x\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ for all real $x$, showing its behavior as $x \to +\infty$ and $x \to -\infty$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using your sketch, determine the number of real roots of the equation $x\mathrm{e}^{-x} = k$ for each of the following cases: (i) $k = \dfrac{1}{2\mathrm{e}}$, (ii) $k = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$, (iii) $k = 1$, and (iv) $k = -1$.

figure.purpose: Show y = x e^(-x) with maximum at (1, 1/e) and horizontal lines y = k.
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = x e^(-x) with horizontal lines showing 0, 1, or 2 roots.
figure.brief: Full axes. Curve y = x e^(-x) passing through origin (0,0), maximum at (1, e^(-1)), approaching y = 0 as x -> +infinity, and plunging to -infinity as x -> -infinity. Horizontal reference lines at y = 1/e, y = 1/(2e), y = 1, y = -1.

questions.prompt: The curve $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}$ is defined for $x > 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: By differentiating $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}$, find the exact coordinates of its maximum turning point. Sketch the curve $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}$ for $x > 0$, stating the coordinates of the point where it crosses the $x$-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Given that $\mathrm{e}^{-1} \approx 0.368 > \dfrac{1}{3}$, deduce the number of real roots of $\dfrac{\ln x}{x} = \dfrac{1}{3}$, and locate each root between consecutive integers.

figure.purpose: Show y = (ln x)/x peaking at (e, 1/e) and intersecting y = 1/3 at two points.
figure.alt_text: Graph of y = (ln x)/x and y = 1/3 with two intersection points.
figure.brief: Axes for x > 0. Curve passes through (1,0), reaches maximum at (e, 1/e) approx (2.718, 0.368), and asymptotes to y = 0 as x -> infinity. Horizontal line y = 1/3 intersects curve at x in (2,3) and x in (4,5).
